title: Liquid Gold Rush: How Ghee Became a $62 Billion Global Phenomenon — and Why Your Nani Saw It Coming
excerpt: North America is now the fastest-growing ghee market in the world, driven by keto diets, Ayurvedic wellness trends, and a diaspora that never stopped cooking with it.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • The global ghee market is projected to reach $82.26 billion by 2031.
  • North America is the fastest-growing ghee market, expanding at a 7.48% CAGR.
  • Organic ghee exports from India increased by 27% in 2024.
  • Premium grass-fed ghee variants are priced 30-50% higher than commodity ghee.
  • Cultural rebranding of ghee raises concerns among the Indian diaspora.

A new kitchen trend is making waves across Western social media — melting butter slowly until it turns aromatic and nutty, a process influencers are hailing as a "butter glow-up." For the billions of people across South Asia who have been doing this for roughly five thousand years, the reaction lands somewhere between a knowing smile and a gentle eye-roll. The ingredient in question is ghee, and it is having a moment that its most devoted fans — Indian grandmothers — always knew was inevitable. ## From Rigveda to Retail Shelf Ghee has been an integral part of Indian cooking, Ayurveda, and religious rituals since the Vedic period. References to clarified butter appear in the Rigveda, one of humanity's oldest texts, and its role in Hindu ceremonies — from lamp lighting to marriage rituals — gives it a cultural weight that no trendy superfood label can fully capture. But outside South Asian kitchens, ghee spent decades in obscurity, dismissed as just another saturated fat during the low-fat diet era of the 1980s and 1990s. That perception has now reversed spectacularly. The global ghee market reached an estimated $62.46 billion in 2026, according to Mordor Intelligence, and is projected to hit $82.26 billion by 2031, growing at a compound annual rate of 5.66 percent. The most striking data point, however, is geographic: North America is now the fastest-growing ghee market on the planet, expanding at a 7.48 percent CAGR — outpacing even Asia-Pacific, where ghee has been a household staple for millennia. ## The Keto Effect What changed? The rise of keto, paleo, and Whole30 diets gave ghee an unlikely second life among Western health-conscious consumers. Nutritionists began highlighting its high smoke point (around 485°F, higher than most cooking oils), its natural lactose-free status after the milk solids are removed, and the gut-friendly butyric acid it contains. Suddenly, ghee was not an exotic ethnic ingredient but a "clean-label, high-smoke-point fat" competing directly with coconut oil and avocado oil in the premium cooking segment. Premium grass-fed and A2 ghee variants, the kind sourced from cows raised on organic pastures, now command prices 30 to 50 percent higher than commodity ghee in North American and European retail. Brands like Fourth & Heart, Tin Star Foods, and Ancient Organics have carved out shelf space at Whole Foods, Costco, and Target. Pure Indian Foods, a New Jersey-based family company, sells a turmeric-infused "Superghee" that is USDA Organic, Whole30 Approved, and Certified Keto — a label trifecta that would have been inconceivable a decade ago. ## India's Export Surge Indian producers are paying attention. Amul, the dairy cooperative that is a household name across India, reported a 27 percent year-over-year increase in organic ghee exports in 2024, with rising demand in the United States, United Arab Emirates, and Australia driving the numbers. Fortune Business Insights projects the global ghee market will grow from $67.75 billion in 2026 to nearly $116 billion by 2034, exhibiting a CAGR of 6.95 percent. The premiumisation trend is real. Organic ghee is projected to grow at a 7.86 percent CAGR through 2031, nearly double the overall market rate. Grass-fed formulations and A2 variants — made from the milk of indigenous Indian cow breeds like Gir and Sahiwal — are commanding the highest premiums.

## The Rebranding Problem Not everyone in the diaspora is thrilled about the way this adoption is playing out. Western brands have a tendency to repackage Indian ingredients under new names — turmeric became "golden milk," yoga became a fitness class, and ghee is now frequently marketed as "clarified butter" at premium prices that would astonish anyone who grew up buying Amul or Patanjali tins at a fraction of the cost. "This is not the first time Indian ingredients have been rediscovered and marketed for a global audience," the trade publication Agro & Food Processing observed. "Turmeric, long used in Indian households, became a 'superfood' in Western wellness circles, while yoga transformed from a spiritual practice into a mainstream fitness trend. Now, ghee is undergoing a similar transformation." For NRIs, the emotional calculus is complicated. There is pride in seeing an ancestral ingredient validated on a global stage, but also a familiar frustration when the cultural context is stripped away and the price tag inflated. ## What Comes Next

The category's future depends on whether Indian brands can capture more of the premium segment rather than ceding it to Western startups. India accounts for 76 percent of global ghee production by volume, but the value capture on exports remains disproportionately low. Companies like Amul, Patanjali, and a growing number of D2C brands like Anveshan and Two Brothers Organic are pushing into the US and European retail markets with products that carry both the premiumisation markers Western consumers want and the cultural authenticity that makes the product meaningful. For the Indian grandmother who never stopped adding a generous spoonful of ghee to dal, to parathas, to rice, to everything — the West has finally caught up. She was never waiting for the validation.
